sections.history: Omampuliyur lies in the Kattumannarkoil country of present-day Cuddalore district, on the northern bank of the Kollidam, in the old Chola heartland north of the Kaveri. Both Sambandar and Appar sang the Lord of this place in the seventh-century Tevaram, one hymn each, and the shrine is therefore a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Sambandar knew the town as Om-Ampuliyur, the town of the sacred syllable, while Appar heard in its name the homa smoke that rose from the sacrificial fires of its sages. It is also counted among the five Puliyur shrines linked to the tiger-footed sage Vyaghrapada, whence the Lord is called Pranava Vyakrapureeswarar. The present stone temple is the work of medieval Tamil patrons whose names are not firmly recorded.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram. In the front mandapa, panels illustrate the sacred legend of the place for those who walk in. The sanctum of Thuyar Theertha Nathar holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess Poongodi Nayaki, whose name means the flowering vine, is honoured in her own shrine. The great distinction of the temple is that Dakshinamurthy, the divine teacher, is enshrined within the sanctum itself, a rarity among Shiva temples. On the walls of the sanctum are the usual niche figures of Vinayaka, Dakshinamurthy, Lingodbhava, Brahma, Vishnu and Durga, and a sculpted panel shows Shiva blessing Vishnu with the discus. A shrine to Murugan stands in the courtyard. The sacred tree is the ilanthai.
sections.legends: The legend of Omampuliyur is a story of teaching. The goddess asked her Lord to explain the meaning of the Pranava, the sacred syllable Om, and Shiva, appearing as Dakshinamurthy, gave her the true teaching at this place; from this the town is said to take its name. Another tradition adds that the goddess came down to earth here and prayed to be restored to her Lord's grace. The sage Vyaghrapada, who worshipped here before going on to witness the cosmic dance at Chidambaram, belongs to the same story. As Thuyar Theertha Nathar, the Lord who ends sorrow, he is approached by those whose hearts are heavy. Because the divine teacher abides in the sanctum, the Lord here is honoured first as the guru, and the temple is regarded as a place for relief from the troubles said to follow the planet Jupiter.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps Thai Poosam in January or February, Masi Magam in February or March, Navaratri in the autumn and Maha Shivaratri, observed as at every Shiva temple. The Jupiter transit, known as Guru Peyarchi, is celebrated here with special devotion, as befits a Guru shrine. Monthly Pradosham is also observed. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Omampuliyur is a place for a still and attentive visit. Enter beneath the three-tiered gopuram, look at the panels in the front mandapa that tell the story of the place, and come to the sanctum of Thuyar Theertha Nathar, where Dakshinamurthy stands within the shrine as the silent teacher. Then walk to the goddess Poongodi Nayaki and to the shrine of Murugan in the courtyard. Students, those seeking wisdom and those carrying a private sorrow come here in particular. The village lies in quiet countryside near the Kollidam, and the temple keeps the calm of a very old sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6:00 am until noon and again from about 4:00 pm until 8:00 pm; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Omampuliyur is a village in Kattumannarkoil taluk, Cuddalore district, on the northern bank of the Kollidam, roughly 15 km east of Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Buses reach the village from Kattumannarkoil and Chidambaram, and Mayiladuthurai is also within easy reach. Chidambaram and Mayiladuthurai are the nearest major railway towns, and Tiruchirappalli is the nearest major airport.
